A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same trajectory-recovery work, renamed from PTR to PLMTrajRec. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support a complete comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Chengdu and Porto experiments, including benchmark comparisons, limited-data experiments, ablations, convergence curves, hyperparameter studies and computational costs.

after.justification: v2 retains original Chengdu and Porto results and adds baseline comparisons, a held-out sampling-interval experiment and randomly initialized BERT ablations.

M1.justification: The prompt contents, Fourier and road features, road-condition interpolation, reference-token attention, BERT/LoRA encoder, losses and joint training followed by interval-specific fine-tuning remain the same. The renamed IF-guided, AF-guided and road condition passing components correspond to existing procedures; the corrected trajectory-length formula matches v1's endpoint-inclusive Figure 4.

E1.justification: Both versions use Chengdu and Porto trajectories with 1-, 2- and 4-minute sparse inputs and 15-second recovery targets. The new zero-shot experiment withholds an existing interval during training; it changes the protocol within retained coverage rather than adding a dataset, population or recovery task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds TERI + Decoder and TrajBERT + Decoder across both datasets and all three intervals, retaining the ten original baselines from v1 Table 1. Appendix A explains their adaptation using MTrajRec's decoder, with only TERI's second stage used.

E3.justification: v2 adds a distinct generalization protocol: training on 1- and 4-minute trajectories and testing on the withheld 2-minute interval. It also introduces a randomly initialized BERT control. These materially extend the evaluation design; the retained experiments preserve their data split, metrics, sampling settings and training budget.

E4.justification: Section 5.7 newly tests generalization to an interval absent from training, and Tables 5 and 8 test the contribution of language-model pretraining. Conversely, v1's convergence analysis and Figures 5–6 are removed. Existing component ablations, data-size analyses, hyperparameter studies and trajectory case study remain, partly relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The percentage declines added in v2 Table 4 describe performance differences, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark, scalability, ablation and computational-cost values are unchanged. v2 adds TERI/TrajBERT results, zero-shot Chengdu results including 79.62% accuracy and 379.6 m RMSE, and random-BERT accuracies of 74.11% on Chengdu and 62.06% on Porto versus the pretrained model's 81.76% and 66.40%. The convergence curves are removed. These substantially extend the reported findings without improving the retained benchmark scores.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a short Fourier-feature inner-product derivation, Equation 19, where v1 offered only intuition. v2 also corrects the trajectory-length expression and projection-matrix dimensions. The new derivation's replacement of learned projections and frequencies by scalar norms is invalid for the unrestricted weights defined in the paper.

C1.justification: The central limited-data recovery and cross-interval generalization claims remain. The contribution summary replaces v1's state-of-the-art accuracy-and-efficiency claim with effectiveness, scalability and generalizability, and foregrounds inference of missing-point road conditions as a distinct contribution.

C2.justification: v2 attributes the smaller held-out-interval degradation to its prompts and joint training, contrasting this with baselines' difficulty handling changed temporal dynamics. It also interprets the random-initialization ablation as evidence for pretraining's value. The previous discussion of rapid convergence is removed; most existing interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly specifies four BERT-small transformer layers and adds a foundation-model source link; BERT-small and the 512-dimensional setting were already disclosed in v1. Appendix C adds a worked prompt and defines its distance feature, while Appendix A documents the new baseline adaptations. These are documentation additions, not evidence of a backbone change.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on multi-rate time series and message passing, plus LightTR, TEST and DeepMM, while removing the trajectory-survey and TPLLM references. It also acknowledges that MM-STGED incorporates observed-point road conditions, sharpening the distinction around conditions at missing points. The overall research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and methodological overview are extensively rewritten around revised challenge descriptions and component terminology. The title and model are renamed, explicit research-question labels are removed, related-work headings are condensed, and appendices are reorganized to separate prompt examples, Fourier-feature reasoning and variant descriptions.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the displays: the dataset table moves into the main text; scalability and ablation tables are split between main text and appendices; a zero-shot table and new comparison rows are added; and the two convergence figures disappear. Architecture labels and captions are revised, while the retained hyperparameter plots and trajectory case study are relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The held-out-interval experiment and random-initialization control directly test generalization and pretraining benefits that v1 supported less directly. Additional baselines and clearer implementation details also strengthen the empirical paper. These gains are tempered by removal of convergence evidence and the invalid factorization introduced in Appendix D, Equation 19, yielding a limited overall improvement.
